title: Tone & Coordination
keywords: tone spasticity grading grade rigidity hypotonia modified ashworth scale mas tardieu coordination cerebellar ataxia finger nose heel shin dysdiadochokinesia
summary: Grade spasticity with the Modified Ashworth and Tardieu scales, tell spasticity from rigidity, and examine coordination and balance — finger-nose, heel-shin, Romberg and more.
ur: Spasticity ko MAS aur Tardieu se grade karna, rigidity se differentiate karna, aur coordination tests sahi tareeqe se karna.

sources.title: O'Sullivan, Schmitz & Fulk — Physical Rehabilitation (7th ed.)

goals.beginner: Know what tone is and what each coordination test checks.
goals.intermediate: Perform MAS, Tardieu and coordination tests correctly.
goals.advanced: Separate spasticity, rigidity, cerebellar and sensory ataxia.
goals.expert: Use findings to guide treatment and pass neuro OSCE stations.

concepts.title: What is muscle tone?
concepts.body: Tone is the **resistance you feel when you move a relaxed limb**. Too little (hypotonia) feels floppy — LMN or cerebellar problems. Too much (hypertonia) is either **spasticity** or **rigidity**.
concepts.ur: Tone = rest par limb ko passively move karne par feel hone wali resistance.

concepts.title: Spasticity vs rigidity

head: Spasticity
Rigidity
rows: Mostly one direction (arm flexors, leg extensors)

concepts.body: The speed test is the key: move fast, then slow.

concepts.title: Modified Ashworth Scale — method
concepts.body: Position the patient relaxed and supported. Move the limb through its **full available range in about one second**. Grade what you feel; repeat no more than three times (repetition reduces tone).

head: Grade
Description
rows: Slight increase: catch and release or minimal resistance at the end of range
Slight increase: catch, then minimal resistance through less than half of the range
Marked increase through most of the range, but the part moves easily

concepts.title: Coordination tests
concepts.body: Test the arms (finger-to-nose, rapid alternating movements) and the legs (heel-to-shin), then balance (Romberg, tandem gait). Do them with eyes open and closed: incoordination that worsens dramatically with eyes closed is **sensory**, not cerebellar.

concepts.title: Cerebellar signs (DANISH)
concepts.body: Hemispheric lesions affect the limbs on the same side; midline (vermis) lesions affect trunk and gait.

concepts.title: What Romberg really tests
concepts.body: Romberg is positive only when the patient is **steady with eyes open but unsteady with eyes closed** — vision was compensating for lost proprioception. A patient unsteady with eyes open has cerebellar or vestibular ataxia; the test is then not interpretable as 'positive'.

concepts.title: From findings to treatment
concepts.body: A large Tardieu R2−R1 gap means the limitation is mostly neural — positioning, stretching, splinting and (medically) botulinum toxin may help. A small gap with reduced R2 means contracture — serial casting or surgery may be needed. Cerebellar ataxia responds to task practice with weights, visual cues and balance training; sensory ataxia to vision, proprioceptive training and safe environments.

questions.prompt: Spasticity is…

Reduced tone
Normal tone
The same at all speeds

questions.prompt: Rigidity is typical of…

Parkinson's disease
Stroke
Peripheral neuropathy

questions.prompt: MAS grade 1+ means…

Rigid limb
Marked increase through most of the range

options: Over 10 seconds
As slowly as possible
Through full range in about one second

questions.prompt: In the Tardieu scale, R1 is…

The angle of catch with fast stretch
Active range
The resting angle

Tremor at rest
Overshooting a target

Normal

Positive Romberg — sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia

questions.prompt: Right-sided intention tremor and dysmetria suggest a lesion in the…

Left motor cortex
Right dorsal columns

questions.prompt: Ratchety resistance at the wrist that doesn't change with speed =
options: Contracture
Cogwheel rigidity

Clonus

questions.prompt: Pronator drift indicates…

Normal fatigue
Peripheral nerve lesion
Cerebellar disease only

questions.case: Elbow flexors after stroke: slow PROM extension to 0° (R2), fast stretch catch at 60° (R1).
questions.prompt: What does the large gap suggest?
options: Fixed contracture
Rigidity
No spasticity
Mostly dynamic (neural) spasticity — may respond to stretching/toxin
questions.explain: R2−R1 = 60° dynamic component.

questions.case: Wide-based staggering gait, can't tandem walk, limbs coordinate normally lying down.
questions.prompt: Lesion?
options: Midline (vermis) cerebellum
Dorsal columns
Cerebellar hemisphere
Peripheral neuropathy
questions.explain: Truncal/gait ataxia with normal limbs = vermis.

questions.prompt: Which finding best separates spasticity from rigidity?
options: The patient's age
Whether resistance changes with stretch speed
Reflex hammer type
Muscle bulk
questions.explain: Spasticity is velocity-dependent; rigidity is not.

questions.case: Numb feet, absent ankle reflexes, unsteady in the dark, positive Romberg.
questions.prompt: Most helpful treatment focus?
options: Visual compensation, proprioceptive and balance training, safe home lighting
Spasticity stretching only
Bed rest
Botulinum toxin
questions.explain: Sensory ataxia: train balance and compensate with vision.

questions.case: Stroke: MAS 3 in the plantarflexors; slow PROM dorsiflexion stops at −10° (cannot reach neutral).
questions.prompt: What does this add?
options: Pure dynamic spasticity
Rigidity
Normal tone
A fixed contracture component is present — stretching/serial casting or orthotic needed, toxin alone won't restore range
questions.explain: If slow passive range (R2) is limited, soft-tissue shortening exists alongside spasticity.

questions.case: Resistance increases on fast elbow extension, with a clasp-knife release near end range.
questions.prompt: Pattern?
options: Gegenhalten (paratonia)
Lead-pipe rigidity
Spasticity (UMN)
Hypotonia
questions.explain: Velocity dependence and the clasp-knife phenomenon are classic spasticity.

questions.case: An older adult with dementia: resistance that increases the harder you try to move the limb, in any direction.
questions.prompt: Most likely?
options: Contracture
Paratonia (gegenhalten)
Spasticity
Cogwheel rigidity
questions.explain: Paratonia matches the examiner's force and is seen with frontal-lobe/diffuse disease.

questions.case: Heel-to-shin test is clumsy only with eyes closed; finger-to-nose is normal.
questions.prompt: Most likely cause?
options: Vermis lesion
Parkinson's disease
Lower-limb proprioceptive loss (sensory ataxia)
Cerebellar hemisphere lesion
questions.explain: Cerebellar ataxia does not improve much with vision; sensory ataxia worsens without it.

questions.prompt: When should MAS be re-tested to judge a botulinum toxin injection?
options: Immediately after the injection
Any position is fine

Same position, same speed, same time of day, by the same assessor — about 4–6 weeks after injection
questions.explain: Toxin peaks at ~4–6 weeks; standardisation is essential for MAS reliability.

cards.front: What does the Modified Ashworth Scale test?
cards.back: Resistance to passive stretch (spasticity) graded 0, 1, 1+, 2, 3, 4

cards.front: How do you perform the Modified Ashworth Scale?
cards.back: Patient relaxed (often supine); move the limb through full range in about one second; grade the resistance felt.

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Modified Ashworth Scale?
cards.back: Catch, resistance through range or rigidity (grades 1–4)

cards.front: What does an abnormal Modified Ashworth Scale suggest?
cards.back: Spasticity from an upper motor neuron lesion (stroke, SCI, MS, cerebral palsy)

cards.front: What does the Modified Tardieu Scale test?
cards.back: Velocity-dependent spasticity: the angle of catch versus full passive range

cards.front: How do you perform the Modified Tardieu Scale?
cards.back: Move the joint slowly (V1) to find full PROM (R2), then as fast as possible (V3) to find the angle of catch (R1).

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Modified Tardieu Scale?
cards.back: A catch (R1) well before the end of slow range (R2)

cards.front: What does an abnormal Modified Tardieu Scale suggest?
cards.back: A large R2−R1 gap = dynamic spasticity (may respond to stretching/botulinum toxin); small gap = contracture

cards.front: What does the Clonus test?
cards.back: Hyperexcitable stretch reflex

cards.front: How do you perform the Clonus?
cards.back: Briskly dorsiflex the foot (or push the patella down) and hold.

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Clonus?
cards.back: Rhythmic beats — sustained (more than about 3–5) is abnormal

cards.front: What does an abnormal Clonus suggest?
cards.back: Upper motor neuron lesion

cards.front: What does the Lead-pipe rigidity test?
cards.back: Uniform resistance through range regardless of speed

cards.front: How do you perform the Lead-pipe rigidity?
cards.back: Move the limb slowly and quickly through full range; compare.

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Lead-pipe rigidity?
cards.back: Constant 'bending a lead pipe' resistance in both directions

cards.front: What does an abnormal Lead-pipe rigidity suggest?
cards.back: Extrapyramidal disorder (e.g. Parkinson's disease, neuroleptic side effects)

cards.front: What does the Cogwheel rigidity test?
cards.back: Rigidity with a superimposed tremor

cards.front: How do you perform the Cogwheel rigidity?
cards.back: Slowly flex and extend or rotate the wrist; feel for ratchet-like jerks.

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Cogwheel rigidity?
cards.back: A ratchety, catch-release-catch feel through range

cards.front: What does an abnormal Cogwheel rigidity suggest?
cards.back: Parkinson's disease (rigidity + tremor)

cards.front: What does the Finger-to-nose test test?
cards.back: Accuracy and smoothness of arm movement (cerebellar function)

cards.front: How do you perform the Finger-to-nose test?
cards.back: Patient touches their nose then your finger, repeatedly; move your finger to new positions.

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Finger-to-nose test?
cards.back: Dysmetria (overshooting/undershooting) and intention tremor near the target

cards.front: What does an abnormal Finger-to-nose test suggest?
cards.back: Ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion; also sensory ataxia if worse with eyes closed

cards.front: What does the Rapid alternating movements test?
cards.back: Ability to switch quickly between opposing movements

cards.front: How do you perform the Rapid alternating movements?
cards.back: Patient pats one hand alternately with the palm and back of the other hand as fast as possible.

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Rapid alternating movements?
cards.back: Slow, irregular, clumsy alternation (dysdiadochokinesia)

cards.front: What does an abnormal Rapid alternating movements suggest?
cards.back: Cerebellar lesion (same side)

cards.front: What does the Heel-to-shin test test?
cards.back: Lower-limb coordination (cerebellar)

cards.front: How do you perform the Heel-to-shin test?
cards.back: Supine: place one heel on the opposite knee and slide it down the shin to the ankle, then back.

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Heel-to-shin test?
cards.back: Heel wobbles off the shin, overshoots or tremors

cards.front: What does an abnormal Heel-to-shin test suggest?
cards.back: Ipsilateral cerebellar lesion; sensory ataxia if much worse with eyes closed

cards.front: What does the Romberg test test?
cards.back: Proprioception (dorsal columns) — not the cerebellum

cards.front: How do you perform the Romberg test?
cards.back: Standing, feet together, arms by the sides; eyes open then closed for 30 seconds; stand close to guard.

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Romberg test?
cards.back: Stable with eyes open but sways or falls with eyes closed

cards.front: What does an abnormal Romberg test suggest?
cards.back: Sensory ataxia: dorsal column or large-fibre neuropathy (e.g. B12 deficiency, diabetes)

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Tandem gait?

cards.front: What does an abnormal Tandem gait suggest?

cards.front: What does the Pronator drift test?

cards.front: How do you perform the Pronator drift?
cards.back: Arms outstretched, palms up, eyes closed for 20–30 seconds.

cards.front: What is an abnormal finding in the Pronator drift?
cards.back: One arm pronates and drifts downward

cards.front: What does an abnormal Pronator drift suggest?
cards.back: Contralateral UMN (pyramidal) lesion

cards.front: Spasticity is…
cards.back: Velocity-dependent increase in tone. Faster stretch = more resistance.

cards.front: Rigidity is typical of…
cards.back: Parkinson's disease. Extrapyramidal disorders cause rigidity.

cards.front: The finger-to-nose test checks…
cards.back: Coordination (cerebellar function). Accuracy and smoothness of movement.

cards.front: Hypotonia (floppy limb) suggests…
cards.back: LMN or cerebellar problem. Reduced tone = LMN, cerebellar or acute spinal shock.

cards.front: MAS grade 1+ means…
cards.back: Catch followed by minimal resistance through less than half of the range. 1+ adds minimal resistance after the catch.

cards.front: How fast should you move the limb for MAS?
cards.back: Through full range in about one second. Standard speed ≈ 1 second.

cards.front: In the Tardieu scale, R1 is…
cards.back: The angle of catch with fast stretch. R1 = catch at fast velocity; R2 = full slow PROM.

cards.front: Dysdiadochokinesia is…
cards.back: Impaired rapid alternating movements. A cerebellar sign.

cards.front: Steady with eyes open, falls with eyes closed:
cards.back: Positive Romberg — sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia. Vision was compensating for lost proprioception.

cards.front: Right-sided intention tremor and dysmetria suggest a lesion in the…
cards.back: Right cerebellar hemisphere. Cerebellar hemisphere lesions affect the same side.

cards.front: Ratchety resistance at the wrist that doesn't change with speed =
cards.back: Cogwheel rigidity. Rigidity with superimposed tremor.

cards.front: Pronator drift indicates…
cards.back: A subtle contralateral UMN lesion. The weak arm pronates and drifts down.

cards.front: Elbow flexors after stroke: slow PROM extension to 0° (R2), fast stretch catch at 60° (R1). — What does the large gap suggest?
cards.back: Mostly dynamic (neural) spasticity — may respond to stretching/toxin. R2−R1 = 60° dynamic component.

cards.front: Wide-based staggering gait, can't tandem walk, limbs coordinate normally lying down. — Lesion?
cards.back: Midline (vermis) cerebellum. Truncal/gait ataxia with normal limbs = vermis.

cards.front: Which finding best separates spasticity from rigidity?
cards.back: Whether resistance changes with stretch speed. Spasticity is velocity-dependent; rigidity is not.

cards.front: Numb feet, absent ankle reflexes, unsteady in the dark, positive Romberg. — Most helpful treatment focus?
cards.back: Visual compensation, proprioceptive and balance training, safe home lighting. Sensory ataxia: train balance and compensate with vision.

cards.front: Stroke: MAS 3 in the plantarflexors; slow PROM dorsiflexion stops at −10° (cannot reach neutral). — What does this add?
cards.back: A fixed contracture component is present — stretching/serial casting or orthotic needed, toxin alone won't restore range. If slow passive range (R2) is limited, soft-tissue shortening exists alongside spasticity.

cards.front: Resistance increases on fast elbow extension, with a clasp-knife release near end range. — Pattern?
cards.back: Spasticity (UMN). Velocity dependence and the clasp-knife phenomenon are classic spasticity.

cards.front: An older adult with dementia: resistance that increases the harder you try to move the limb, in any direction. — Most likely?
cards.back: Paratonia (gegenhalten). Paratonia matches the examiner's force and is seen with frontal-lobe/diffuse disease.

cards.front: Heel-to-shin test is clumsy only with eyes closed; finger-to-nose is normal. — Most likely cause?
cards.back: Lower-limb proprioceptive loss (sensory ataxia). Cerebellar ataxia does not improve much with vision; sensory ataxia worsens without it.

cards.front: When should MAS be re-tested to judge a botulinum toxin injection?
cards.back: Same position, same speed, same time of day, by the same assessor — about 4–6 weeks after injection. Toxin peaks at ~4–6 weeks; standardisation is essential for MAS reliability.

cards.front: Modified Ashworth Scale — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: It does not separate neural spasticity from stiff soft tissue — combine with Tardieu and PROM.

cards.front: Modified Tardieu Scale — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: Speed must be standardised and the same angle measured each time.

cards.front: Clonus — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: A few unsustained beats can occur in anxious or brisk normal people.

cards.front: Lead-pipe rigidity — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: Ask the patient to move the other limb (activation) to bring out subtle rigidity.

cards.front: Cogwheel rigidity — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: Don't confuse with spasticity — rigidity is not velocity-dependent and affects both directions.

cards.front: Finger-to-nose test — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: Severe weakness can mimic incoordination — check power first.

cards.front: Rapid alternating movements — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: Compare with the non-dominant side normally being slightly slower.

cards.front: Heel-to-shin test — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: Hip or knee pain and weakness affect performance.

cards.front: Romberg test — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: Patients with cerebellar ataxia are unstable even with eyes open — that is not a positive Romberg.

cards.front: Tandem gait — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: Often impaired in normal older adults — interpret with age.

cards.front: Pronator drift — pitfall: what must you remember?
cards.back: Upward drift without pronation suggests a parietal (proprioceptive) or cerebellar problem.
